The pattern to track isn't what he says, it's the ratio of promised things to completed things.

threads.title: The Trip That Lives in the Notes App
threads.note: He loves planning the trip, but no step of the planning ever involves a payment or a date.

bubbles.text: ok I just found flights to Lisbon for like $340 round trip. we are SO going
haha stop, that's tempting. when were you thinking?
honestly the second week of May is perfect. we rent a little place near the water, eat pastries every morning, get lost
I'm in. want to book this weekend so the price doesn't jump?
100%. let me just check a couple work things first
Sure. Did you get a chance to check?
ahh slammed this week, I haven't forgotten!! this is happening babe 🇵🇹

threads.title: Meet the Family (Eventually)
threads.note: He hands out promised introductions like gift cards that expire before he'll let you use them.

bubbles.text: my mom is going to adore you. she'd literally be obsessed
That's sweet! I'd love to meet her.
we'll do Sunday dinner at some point, she makes the best lasagna. you'll love my sister too
Is there a Sunday coming up that works?
this one is crazy, my cousin's thing. but soon, I promise
What about the one after?
lol you're so eager, I love it. let's see how the month shakes out 😘
I'm not eager, I'm just taking you at your word.

threads.title: The Small Ask
threads.note: When a plan is asked to be a Thursday instead of a dream, he flinches.

bubbles.text: Hey, quick one. Are you free Thursday for dinner? Just us.
Thursday... ugh, not sure yet, things are chaotic
No worries. Friday or Saturday?
babe I can't even think about this week. but you know what I was thinking about? us doing a whole month in Japan next year
That's a big dream. I'd also like to know about this week.
wow ok. I'm literally telling you I see a future with you and you're mad about a dinner?
I'm not mad. I'm asking for a dinner. Both things can be true.

threads.title: The Comeback Itinerary
threads.note: After going quiet for days, he returns with a bigger promise instead of an explanation.

bubbles.text: I haven't heard from you in four days.
I know, I'm sorry, my head's been a mess. you deserve better than that
I'd like to know what happened.
work and some personal stuff. but listen, I've been thinking about us all week. I want to take you to the lake house this summer, for real, just us
That sounds lovely, but it doesn't answer the four days.
I'm trying to show you where my head is. I'm in this. can we not make it a thing?
I'd like to see you this week, in person, as a start.
ok let me see how it looks 🙏

characters.name: Ted Mosby
characters.why: Ted falls for the idea of a woman and her whole future, often within a single dinner, and narrates it to everyone including his kids. The vision is sweet and sincere, which is exactly what makes it so hard to tell apart from the follow-through he keeps failing to deliver.

characters.name: Don Draper
characters.why: Don is a professional pitchman, and he sells women the same kind of perfect tomorrow he sells clients: vivid, emotional, and unattached to the facts. When the real relationship needs him in the room, he is on a plane or in another bed.

characters.name: Mr. Big
characters.why: Big dangles grand gestures like Paris and a big life together while dodging the plain commitments that would make Carrie feel safe. The grand finale is always more romantic than the Tuesday in between.

characters.name: Jay Gatsby
characters.why: Gatsby is in love with a gorgeous imagined future, and he builds an entire life around it while the actual person in front of him is treated as a prop. His sincerity is never in doubt, and that is exactly why the dream is so costly to stand next to.

interested.point: He talks about next year in the first month.
interested.detail: Real interest can include long-term talk, but his is unusually detailed and early, like picking out the baby's name on date four. If it's matched by actions, wonderful. If it's only words, it's the show, not the interest.

interested.point: He texts you in the late-night glow.
interested.detail: The most elaborate promises land at 11pm or after a great evening, when he's feeling most connected to you. That's genuine feeling in the moment, and it's real, but it tends to fade by morning.

interested.point: He includes you in imaginary scenes with his people.
interested.detail: He'll say your future sister-in-law will love you or that his best friend will tease you at the wedding. He is mentally placing you in his world, even if he hasn't taken a single step to physically do it.

interested.point: He sends you listings, flights, and links.
interested.detail: A screenshot of a cabin rental or a link to a Saturday market is his love language in flirt form. It proves you're on his mind, though it doesn't prove he'll click 'reserve.'

interested.point: He gets visibly emotional when he describes 'us.'
interested.detail: He can tear up while describing a morning in a house you don't own yet. The feeling is often real in that moment, which is why it's so easy to confuse with commitment.

interested.point: He asks for your dreams and folds them into his.
interested.detail: If you mention wanting a garden, he'll say 'we're getting a house with a garden' by the next message. He listens well and reflects it back, which feels like being seen before you've been shown up for.

not_interested.point: The present stays strangely empty.
not_interested.detail: You've heard about Italy for two months and still can't get a Wednesday dinner. A man who wants you takes the easy, available hours, not just the epic ones.

not_interested.point: He goes vague the second you pin a date.
not_interested.detail: You say 'Saturday at 7?' and he replies with 'let me see how the week goes.' His enthusiasm is for the picture, not the appointment.

not_interested.point: He changes the subject to a bigger plan.
not_interested.detail: Ask about this weekend and he'll answer with a vacation next spring. Escalating the fantasy to avoid the small ask is a classic way to avoid accountability.

not_interested.point: He disappears when real life asks something of him.
not_interested.detail: When your car breaks down, you have a bad week, or a friend's birthday needs a plus-one, he's suddenly 'swamped.' The future is a fun place to visit, but he doesn't want to do the inconvenient parts.

not_interested.point: He never introduces you to anyone real.
not_interested.detail: Three months in, you've heard about everyone and met no one. If his friends have never heard your name, the 'we' he describes lives only in your chat.

not_interested.point: He gets wounded when you track the gap.
not_interested.detail: Saying 'you said you'd call' earns an 'I can't believe you're keeping score.' When a reasonable question is treated as an attack, it's usually because the answer is uncomfortable.

red_flags.point: Promises with no dates attached.
red_flags.detail: 'We'll go to Greece someday' costs nothing and commits to nothing. Notice whether any of his promises have ever come with a booking confirmation, a deposit, or a time.

red_flags.point: Milestones that outrun the relationship.
red_flags.detail: Talking about marriage and kids when you've never spent a full weekend together is a sign he's skipping the work. Intimacy built on speed instead of experience tends to collapse under normal weight.

red_flags.point: A trail of unmet small promises.
red_flags.detail: He said he'd fix your shelf, call Tuesday, send you the playlist. If the small ones keep slipping, the big ones are not going to survive.

red_flags.point: He weaponizes the dream when you question it.
red_flags.detail: 'I'm telling you I want a future with you and you're nitpicking?' flips the script so your reasonable need becomes ingratitude. Be wary of any dynamic where asking for follow-through makes you the problem.

red_flags.point: Apology by promise.
red_flags.detail: Every time he lets you down, he repays with an even grander vision instead of a changed behavior. A bigger future is not an apology.

red_flags.point: You're editing your life around a plan that isn't real.
red_flags.detail: If you've held a weekend, turned down a trip, or told friends about 'our summer,' you're investing in a ghost. The red flag is when your actual schedule starts bending around his hypothetical one.

green_flags.point: A promise becomes an action within a week.
green_flags.detail: He says 'let's try that ramen place,' and by Friday there's a reservation and a text confirming it. Words converting to calendar entries is the whole test.

green_flags.point: He's comfortable with small, boring plans.
green_flags.detail: He's just as happy to say 'come over Wednesday, I'll make pasta' as to describe a honeymoon. Present-tense interest is the surest proof that the future talk is grounded.

green_flags.point: He names the limits of what he can promise.
green_flags.detail: 'I can't do that weekend, but I can do the next one' is a man who respects your time. He'd rather under-promise and deliver.

green_flags.point: His friends and family know who you are.
green_flags.detail: Within a reasonable period you've met actual people, or at least they've heard about you by name. A real future involves real witnesses.

green_flags.point: He owns it when he drops the ball.
green_flags.detail: He says 'I said I'd call and didn't, that's on me, here's what I'm doing differently,' and then does it. Accountability followed by changed behavior is the opposite of the Future Faker's fog.

what_to_say.line: I love that idea. Can we pick a weekend and book it this week?
what_to_say.why: It meets his enthusiasm warmly and turns it into a test with a deadline. A man who means it will happily say yes, and one who doesn't will show you quickly.

what_to_say.line: I'd love to meet your sister. What Sunday works?
what_to_say.why: It takes his casual promise at face value and asks for a date. You aren't accusing him of anything, just inviting the plan to become real.

what_to_say.line: I like hearing about the future, and I also need the present to match. What are we doing this week?
what_to_say.why: It affirms the dream while naming the actual need. It's calm and clear, which makes it hard to turn into a fight.

what_to_say.line: I'm going to go by what you do over the next month, not what you say.
what_to_say.why: It sets a standard without drama and quietly takes the power out of the promises. You're no longer waiting on his words, you're watching his actions.

what_to_say.line: That's the third trip we've talked about and none is booked. What's getting in the way?
what_to_say.why: It's factual, non-accusatory, and invites a real answer. Whatever he says, you'll learn something about whether he'll face the gap.

never_say.line: You promised me!
never_say.why: It turns a pattern into a one-off argument and gives him a chance to focus on your tone instead of his follow-through. State the facts calmly instead.

never_say.line: I'll plan the whole trip, you just show up.
never_say.why: You become the unpaid project manager of his promise, and he gets the credit for a plan he never made. If the effort isn't shared, the plan isn't mutual.

never_say.line: I guess we can do it whenever you're ready.
never_say.why: An open-ended wait is exactly the environment he thrives in. Without a boundary, 'whenever' becomes 'never.'

never_say.line: Do you even want to be with me?
never_say.why: It invites a dramatic reassurance, which he is exceptionally good at giving. You'll walk away soothed and with no new facts.

never_say.line: I already told my friends we're going to Italy.
never_say.why: It shows how much you've invested in a plan he hasn't, and hands him leverage in the form of your embarrassment. Keep your real commitments to the real things.

manipulation.name: The Movie Trailer
manipulation.how_it_works: He paints a hyper-specific future so vividly that your brain files it as a memory already half-lived. The detail creates emotional investment before any evidence exists.
manipulation.defense: Ask 'when' and 'who books it' every time. Judge the plan by logistics, not imagery.

manipulation.name: The Bigger Promise
manipulation.how_it_works: When you raise a missed commitment, he answers with an even grander plan. The new dream shifts the focus away from the letdown.
manipulation.defense: Return to the original thing: 'I'd still like to talk about the Saturday you missed.' Don't let a bigger promise overwrite a smaller broken one.

manipulation.name: The Trust Trap
manipulation.how_it_works: He recasts your reasonable need for proof as a lack of faith in him. 'If you trusted me, you wouldn't need dates' makes your boundary look like betrayal.
manipulation.defense: Remember that trust is built by consistency, not demanded in advance. Say, 'I trust what I can see. Show me.'

manipulation.name: The Rolling Reschedule
manipulation.how_it_works: Plans are pushed back gently and indefinitely, always with warmth and a new vague target. Each delay seems reasonable, so you never get to a clear moment of 'this is a pattern.'
manipulation.defense: Keep a private tally of dates he's offered and what happened. Patterns are hard to deny when you see them in a list.

manipulation.name: The Sacrifice Shuffle
manipulation.how_it_works: You gradually adjust your own life, turning down invitations and pausing goals, to make room for the future he's described. The more you've given up, the harder it is to question him.
manipulation.defense: Keep living your actual life as though the plans don't exist until they have a receipt. Commit your time only to what is on the calendar.

leverage.point: His own words are your best measuring stick.
leverage.detail: You don't need to accuse him of anything, just reference what he's said and ask for the next step. 'You mentioned May, so which weekend?' makes his talk the standard he's judged by.

leverage.point: Concrete requests are the cleanest test.
leverage.detail: A small, specific ask (Thursday, 7pm, this restaurant) either gets a yes or reveals the gap in minutes. You don't have to argue your case when the data speaks.

leverage.point: A timeline is a boundary he can't spin.
leverage.detail: Saying 'I'm looking for something that shows up in real life within the month' sets a gentle deadline. He can meet it or not, and both answers are useful.

leverage.point: Your full, busy life shifts the dynamic.
leverage.detail: When you have plans, friends, and momentum of your own, his flaky futures lose their pull. He often becomes more present when he senses he can't take your availability for granted, and if he doesn't, you've lost very little.

leverage.point: Your willingness to walk is the real power.
leverage.detail: You can enjoy the warmth while refusing to build on it until it's proven. 'I'm happy to wait for what's real, but I won't wait on what's imaginary' changes the whole conversation.

closest_cousin.text: The Someday Guy and the Future Faker both live in a tomorrow that never arrives, which is why they get confused constantly. The difference is in how the future is packaged. The Someday Guy defers with conditions and a sigh: 'it'll be different when work calms down, when I'm over my ex, when the lease ends.' The Future Faker does the opposite and supplies the future in glittering detail, with the cabin, the dog, and the October leaves, and gives you no reason it isn't happening right now. One sells patience, the other sells a vision, but both leave you holding a promise with no date on it.
closest_cousin.tell: Ask for a date: the Someday Guy answers with a condition ('when things settle'), while the Future Faker answers with enthusiasm and a bigger plan.

nice-guy.identity: He's not kind, he's prepaying. Every favor is a deposit, and one day he'll ask for the balance in affection.
summary: The Nice Guy is the man who holds the door, remembers your coffee order, drives you to the airport at 5 a.m., and fixes your shelf without being asked. On the surface he's a catch, and often he really is generous. The problem is that his generosity comes with a hidden receipt. He isn't giving freely. He's giving toward an outcome, usually you, and he keeps quiet about it until the outcome doesn't arrive. He often describes himself with the word 'nice', which is a tell in itself, because people who are consistently kind rarely need to announce it.

Why does he do it? Nobody can see inside his head, but the pattern suggests he learned that kindness is the safest way to ask for love. Asking directly ('I like you, do you like me back?') risks a clean no. Doing favors feels like a safer route, because if he's helpful enough, surely you'll owe him a yes. So he tries to earn affection by overdelivering instead of risking rejection. Some Nice Guys know they're doing this and some honestly don't. The effect on you is identical either way. The kindness isn't a gift, it's a bid.

Dating him feels wonderful at first and slightly airless later. You get texts like 'Got you that tea you mentioned!', and you feel cared for and a little guilty for not feeling more. Then you notice the sense of owing. You can't say no to his plans without feeling like a villain. You can't date anyone else without it landing like a betrayal. Small disagreements become strangely heavy, because he responds with wounded politeness instead of honesty ('No, it's fine, really'). You start managing his feelings to keep the peace, which is ironic for a man who sells himself as the easy one.

It usually ends one of two ways. Either you say 'I'm just not feeling it', and the sweetness curdles into the invoice: 'After everything I've done for you?' Or you stay out of guilt, and the relationship becomes a slow ledger of resentments with the occasional bouquet. The painful part is that the rejection isn't the cruelty. It's that you were never allowed a clean no, because he made kindness a contract you never signed. The ending line is almost always some version of 'I guess nice guys really do finish last', which tells you he never saw you as a person, just as the prize.

text: His texting rhythm is attentive, warm, and fast. He replies within minutes, asks follow-up questions, remembers the details of your week ('How did the presentation go??'), and fills silences with offers: 'Need anything?', 'Want me to pick something up?', 'Let me know if I can help!' He's rarely the one who disappears, which makes him feel safe. The tell is how often the texts are about service rather than about him. You know what he can do for you, but you rarely get honest opinions, desires, or disagreements. His messages are polished smooth so that nothing in them can be rejected.

Over time the cracks show in the gaps. When you reply slowly, his tone gets a little formal: 'No worries at all!' or 'Totally understand, you're busy.' The exclamation marks multiply as the warmth cools. He starts referencing past favors lightly ('Happy to help, as always'), and the check-ins turn into quiet audits: 'Haven't heard from you in a bit.' If you pull away, he swings between over-apologizing and a sudden, cold accuracy about everything he has done. The shift from 'happy to help' to 'must be nice' can happen inside two texts.

threads.title: The Unrequested Favor
threads.note: He does something huge you didn't ask for, then makes it your emotional debt.

bubbles.text: Hey! Heard you say your car's been making that noise. I booked you in at my guy's garage tomorrow, already paid the deposit 😊
Wait, you did what? I was going to deal with it this weekend
I know, I just hate seeing you stressed. It's done, don't even worry about it
That's really sweet but I'd have liked to be asked first. I can't make tomorrow either
Oh. Okay. No, that's fine.
I rearranged my whole morning to sort it but honestly it's fine!
I'll pay you back for the deposit and sort the time out myself. I didn't ask you to rearrange anything
Wow. Okay. Didn't realize helping was such a crime.

threads.title: The Friend-Zone Invoice
threads.note: A clear no gets answered with an itemized bill of kindness.

bubbles.text: I've been wanting to talk. I really value you, but I'm not feeling romantic about us, and I don't want to lead you on
Okay.
Can I ask what's missing? Because I've been there for you through everything
You have, and I appreciate it. But it doesn't change how I feel
I drove you to the airport twice. I helped you move. I listened to you cry about your ex for months.
I didn't realize those came with conditions. If they did, I wish you'd told me
They don't. I just thought you'd see me differently by now. I guess nice guys really do finish last.
I'm sorry you're hurting. I'm not going to keep the friendship going on those terms though

threads.title: The Mention of Another Guy
threads.note: He doesn't object, he just goes quiet, wounded and passive-aggressive.

bubbles.text: Guess what, I've got a second date with that guy from the climbing gym on Friday!
Oh nice.
Good for you!
Thanks! You okay? That reply felt a bit flat
No, I'm happy for you. Genuinely. I just hope he treats you the way you deserve.
Not everyone is as reliable as the people who've actually been around
Did you just compare yourself to someone you've never met?
Forget I said anything. Have a great date! 🙂

threads.title: The Slow Reply Audit
threads.note: His 'no worries' carries a quiet tally of your availability.

bubbles.text: Hey! Free tonight? Was thinking I'd cook for you 🍝
Can't tonight, work is insane. Rain check?
Of course, no worries at all!
That's the third rain check this week but totally get it
I hear you. I'm swamped and I'm sorry. Thursday?
Thursday works. I'll clear my evening, as always 🙂
You don't need to clear anything. If it doesn't suit you, say so and we'll pick another night
I said it works! I just notice who makes the effort, that's all.

characters.name: Ross Geller
characters.why: Ross spends years being the 'nice guy' who treats his devotion to Rachel as a down payment on her heart, and he's genuinely wounded when it isn't honored. His kindness is real, but it's tangled up with a quiet belief that he's owed an outcome.

characters.name: Ted Mosby
characters.why: Ted performs grand romantic gestures, like the blue French horn, as proof of how good a guy he is. The gestures are often about the story of his own devotion rather than what the woman actually wants.

characters.name: Leonard Hofstadter
characters.why: Leonard is warm, helpful, and constantly doing favors for Penny, and he sometimes lets his resentment show when the affection isn't returned the way he hoped. He regularly frames his niceness as proof he deserves a chance.

characters.name: Tom Hansen
characters.why: Tom is sweet and sincere, but he builds a whole romance in his head and blames Summer when she doesn't follow his script. His hurt comes from the gap between what he gave and what he assumed it would buy.

interested.point: He gives you the best of his time
interested.detail: A Nice Guy who's actually into you will rearrange his week, show up early, and make you the priority. For example, he'll offer to drive across town for dinner, and he'll mean it as an investment rather than as a favor.

interested.point: He remembers everything you say
interested.detail: He'll bring up the stressful meeting you mentioned two weeks ago or the tea you prefer. He's paying close attention because he's building a case for why you two fit.

interested.point: He over-explains his feelings in fragments
interested.detail: He drops lines like 'You're not like other girls' or 'I just really enjoy being around you.' It's affection, but it's often dressed as compliments instead of a direct 'I like you.'

interested.point: He makes himself conveniently available
interested.detail: He's the first to say 'I'm free' and the last to say 'I can't.' If you've got a free Saturday, he's already cleared his.

interested.point: He gets quiet when you mention other men
interested.detail: His warmth cools for a beat when another man enters the story. For example, he asks 'Is he nice to you?' with a tone that doesn't quite sound like a casual question.

interested.point: He hints instead of asking
interested.detail: He'll say 'We should do something sometime' rather than proposing a date with a day and a time. He's testing the waters from behind a safe layer of vagueness.

not_interested.point: His help stays generic
not_interested.detail: When he isn't into you, he'll still be pleasant but won't go out of his way. He'll say 'Let me know if you need anything' and won't offer a specific plan.

not_interested.point: The favors dry up the moment you're unavailable
not_interested.detail: If he's only doing things to earn something, his attention fades once he decides there's no payoff. For example, he stops texting 'good morning' as soon as you start dating someone else.

not_interested.point: He treats you like a friend with a good listening ear
not_interested.detail: He asks about your problems but never shares his own plans for the two of you. The conversation stays about your life, not a future.

not_interested.point: He's warm but never flirts
not_interested.detail: There's no teasing, no lingering looks, no physical edge. He's perfectly nice in a way that never raises the temperature.

not_interested.point: He cancels without apology
not_interested.detail: A man who's lost interest will cancel casually and not scramble to rebook. This is rare for a Nice Guy, so it's a strong signal.

not_interested.point: He gets friendly with your other dates
not_interested.detail: He seems unbothered, even encouraging, about the person you're seeing. It could be genuine peace, or he's decided to back out of the race.

red_flags.point: He says 'I'm a nice guy' about himself
red_flags.detail: People who are consistently kind rarely need to announce it. When he says 'I'm just a nice guy' while explaining why you should date him, he's presenting a credential, not a quality.

red_flags.point: His gifts or favors arrive before you've asked
red_flags.detail: He books the repair, pays the deposit, or buys the concert ticket without checking in. It creates debt you didn't agree to, and when you push back he turns hurt.

red_flags.point: He sulks when you decline
red_flags.detail: A no is met with 'No, it's fine!' in a tone that clearly says otherwise. You learn to avoid declining things, which means you stop being honest.

red_flags.point: He keeps a mental ledger
red_flags.detail: He references what he's done for you in arguments: 'I drove across town when you were sick.' The favors were never gifts, they were entries.

red_flags.point: He can't hear a clear no
red_flags.detail: He asks 'But why?' after you've explained, then offers to change. He's treating your boundary as a problem to solve rather than information to respect.

red_flags.point: He's resentful of your other relationships
red_flags.detail: He's gently dismissive of your male friends or dates, saying things like 'Just be careful, some guys only want one thing.' It's framed as concern but works as quiet competition.

green_flags.point: His generosity doesn't need acknowledgment
green_flags.detail: When he does something nice, he's fine if you simply say thanks and move on. He doesn't bring it up weeks later or expect repayment.

green_flags.point: He can take a no with grace
green_flags.detail: When you turn down plans or a favor, he says 'No problem, another time' and means it. His mood doesn't shift, and you don't have to manage it.

green_flags.point: He states what he wants directly
green_flags.detail: He says 'I'd like to take you on a proper date' instead of hinting. Directness is the opposite of the Nice Guy's strategy and the clearest sign he trusts you with his real feelings.

green_flags.point: He disagrees with you sometimes
green_flags.detail: He'll say 'I see it differently' without collapsing into sulking or giving in. A man who can safely disagree isn't performing agreeableness to earn something.

green_flags.point: He's kind to people who can't do anything for him
green_flags.detail: Watch how he treats waiters, his siblings, and strangers. If the same warmth shows up where there's nothing to gain, it's character instead of strategy.

what_to_say.line: I appreciate that, but please ask me before you do things like that.
what_to_say.why: It names the behavior without attacking him, and it sets a standard for consent around favors. His reaction tells you if the kindness was a gift or a bid.

what_to_say.line: I'm not interested in dating you. I'd rather be clear than keep you hoping.
what_to_say.why: A clean, specific statement leaves no room to negotiate or reinterpret. Kindness here means not letting him wait on a maybe.

what_to_say.line: I don't owe you romance for being kind to me.
what_to_say.why: This names the hidden contract directly. If he's honest, it may land. If he isn't, his defensiveness will confirm what you suspected.

what_to_say.line: If you'd like something from me, just ask me directly.
what_to_say.why: It invites him out of the indirect approach and into honesty. A man with real intentions will find this a relief.

what_to_say.line: Thank you, but I can't accept that. I'd rather pay for myself.
what_to_say.why: It stops the debt before it forms. You're not rejecting him, you're keeping the exchange even.

never_say.line: You're such a good guy, I just don't know why I'm not into you.
never_say.why: This confirms his theory that niceness should have bought you. It invites him to keep trying and fixes nothing.

never_say.line: Maybe things will change, let's see.
never_say.why: Vague hope is fuel for his strategy. He'll keep investing and read every smile as progress.

never_say.line: I'm sorry I'm so bad at this.
never_say.why: Apologizing for having feelings makes you the one at fault. It turns his disappointment into your responsibility.

never_say.line: Sure, you can drive me, I guess I owe you one.
never_say.why: Naming the debt out loud makes it real. You've just agreed to the ledger he was already keeping.

never_say.line: Please don't be mad at me.
never_say.why: This puts you in the role of managing his emotions. His mood becomes the thing you're trying to prevent, which gives him leverage.

manipulation.name: The Pre-Paid Favor
manipulation.how_it_works: He does something big and unrequested, then lets the weight of it sit between you. Saying no later feels rude because he's already spent the effort.
manipulation.defense: Decline favors you didn't ask for, or pay for them yourself right away. If he's hurt by that, the favor was never a gift.

manipulation.name: The Wounded Politeness
manipulation.how_it_works: When he's upset, he says 'No, it's fine!' in a tone that clearly means it isn't. You end up chasing his mood instead of addressing the actual problem.
manipulation.defense: Take him at his word once: 'Okay, if it's fine, then we're good.' Don't dig for the hidden complaint he refuses to state.

manipulation.name: The Selective Memory Ledger
manipulation.how_it_works: He recalls every favor he's done and none of yours. During a disagreement, he pulls out the list as evidence that you're ungrateful.
manipulation.defense: Don't argue the tally. Say, 'I'm grateful, and I'm not going to be in a relationship where kindness gets counted against me.'

manipulation.name: The Victim Pivot
manipulation.how_it_works: When you set a boundary, he reframes it as proof that nice guys get hurt. The conversation shifts from your needs to his pain.
manipulation.defense: Acknowledge his feelings in one sentence, then return to your decision: 'I'm sorry you're hurting, and my answer is the same.'

manipulation.name: The Convenient Friend Trap
manipulation.how_it_works: He stays close as a friend, supportive and available, while quietly hoping you'll change your mind. Your emotional reliance on him keeps the door ajar.
manipulation.defense: Ask yourself if the friendship has an unspoken expectation. If it does, end it or set an honest limit, because it isn't actually friendship yet.

leverage.point: Your clarity is the strongest tool you have
leverage.detail: The Nice Guy depends on ambiguity to keep hoping. One clear sentence like 'I'm not interested romantically' removes his strategy and shows who he really is.

leverage.point: He's usually sincere underneath
leverage.detail: Most Nice Guys aren't villains, they're avoiding rejection. If you stay calm and kind but firm, he may be able to adjust and become a good friend or a better partner to someone else.

leverage.point: Reciprocity is your best test
leverage.detail: Offer small, even exchanges and see how he reacts. For example, cover coffee when he buys lunch, and watch whether he's relaxed or quietly uncomfortable.

leverage.point: His need for approval can be redirected
leverage.detail: A man who wants to be seen as good will often respond when you name the behavior you value. Say 'I love it when you just ask me what I want,' and many will lean into that.

leverage.point: You can always make the exchange transparent
leverage.detail: Saying 'What would you want from me in return?' flushes out the hidden agenda fast. An honest man will answer plainly, and a Nice Guy will realize the invoice has been seen.

closest_cousin.text: The Scorekeeper keeps a ledger of every favor, and the Nice Guy does too, but the two use it differently. The Nice Guy's ledger is quiet and aimed at one outcome, which is your affection, and it comes out when you say no. The Scorekeeper tallies everything across all areas of the relationship (money, chores, texts, who called last) and uses the numbers as ammunition in ordinary arguments, whether or not romance is on the line.
closest_cousin.tell: The Nice Guy presents the bill when you refuse him romantically, while the Scorekeeper presents it whenever he wants to win an argument.

ghost.identity: He's a great first three weeks and a missing-person report after that. The Ghost treats vanishing as a communication style.
summary: The Ghost is the guy who is fully present right up until he isn't. He's usually charming, easy to talk to, and good at the early stuff: the funny first text, the date that runs two hours over, the 'I had a really good time' at the curb. He doesn't come across as a bad guy. He comes across as a normal, pleasant one, and that's why it works. Nothing about him sets off alarms because he hasn't done anything yet. The thing he's best at is the one thing you can't see coming: the exit with no paperwork.

Why he does it is mostly boring, and the boring answer is the truest one. Ending things honestly is uncomfortable, and he's decided his comfort outranks your closure. Some Ghosts are conflict-avoidant and truly believe silence is kinder than a hard conversation. Some got what they wanted (attention, a good time, proof they're still desirable) and lost interest. Some got scared when it started to feel real. Some are juggling three women and you just got dropped from the schedule. We can't know which one he is from the outside, and you don't need to. The behavior is the same, and it tells you what you need: he can't handle an awkward five minutes with someone he claims to like.

Dating him feels like being very warm and then very confused. The early texting has a nice rhythm, so when it thins out, you do the generous thing and invent explanations: work, family stuff, a bad week. You send a casual follow-up that you rewrite four times. You check whether he watched your story (he did). You start to feel like the 'needy' one for noticing that a man who was texting you good morning now can't manage a thumbs-up. That's the cruelest part of the Ghost: he leaves you doing his emotional math for him, and you end up questioning your own reasonable expectations instead of his unreasonable silence.

It usually ends in one of three ways. The clean version is that he stops replying, you stop chasing, and the whole thing dissolves after a few days of you pretending you're fine. The messy version is the resurface weeks later, with a 'hey, sorry, life got crazy' and the confidence of a man who assumes the door is still open. The best version is the one you write yourself: you notice the pattern by the second dip in replies, you say one clear sentence, and you leave before he has a chance to. In every version, the ending was decided the moment he chose silence over a sentence. It says very little about your worth and quite a lot about his capacity.

text: The Ghost's early texting looks great. He replies within the hour, asks follow-up questions, remembers the name of your sister's dog, and sends the occasional 'this reminded me of you.' His rhythm is steady enough that you stop thinking about it, which is exactly why the first change is so easy to miss. The tells show up in the margins: the replies get shorter, the questions stop, the response time stretches from an hour to half a day, and conversations start ending on your message instead of his. He starts answering what you asked but never asks anything back. Plans become 'we should do that soon' with no day attached.

Over time the pattern is a fade, not a cliff. He doesn't go dark all at once; he thins out until the thread is a monologue and you're the only one who sounds invested. You'll notice he's active (liking things, viewing stories, posting) while your last message sits there unanswered, which tells you the problem isn't bandwidth. The final stage is either total silence or a single low-effort reply, like a 'haha' or a 'yeah for sure' that technically counts as an answer and functionally closes the door. If he comes back, it will be after enough days that you've stopped looking, usually with an apology that's casual and a tone that suggests nothing happened.

threads.title: The Slow Fade
threads.note: He never says anything wrong. He just keeps giving less until there's nothing left to answer.

bubbles.text: Okay that restaurant sounds amazing, I'm so in. Thursday?
Thursday works! 7:30?
Perfect. Looking forward to it 😊
Me too. Any allergies I should know about before I book?
nope all good
Great, booked! Want me to send you the address?
yeah sure
Sent it. See you Thursday!

threads.title: The Plan That Evaporates
threads.note: He's enthusiastic about the idea of seeing you and allergic to the actual calendar.

bubbles.text: I'm honestly dying to see you this weekend
Same! Saturday night work for you?
Probably! Let me check a couple things and I'll confirm
Sure. Just let me know by Friday so I can plan around it.
Yep for sure
Hey, Friday night checking in. Are we on for tomorrow?
Totally fine if not, I'd just like to know.
Ahh sorry, crazy day. Maybe next week?

threads.title: The Resurface
threads.note: He shows up after a week of silence with a 'sorry' that skips the part where he explains anything.

bubbles.text: Heyyy stranger. Sorry I've been MIA, work has been insane
Hey. It's been nine days.
I know, I'm the worst 😅 I thought about you though
You watched my story four times, so I'm not sure work was the whole picture.
Wow okay. I didn't realize this was that serious
It's not. I just think when you like someone, you text back. That's all.
Fair enough. Can we start fresh? Drinks this week?
I'm good, thanks. Take care.

threads.title: The Direct Question
threads.note: A clean, calm ask for honesty. His reply is the whole answer.

bubbles.text: Hey, I've noticed the energy shifted on your end. No pressure, but I'd rather know where you're at than guess.
Oh, no, I'm just really busy lately
Totally understandable. Are you still interested in seeing me, or are you winding down?
I mean I like you! Just have a lot going on
Got it. Liking me and making time for me are two different things, and I need the second one.
Yeah I hear you
Okay. I'm going to step back then. Wishing you well.

characters.name: Mr. Big
characters.why: He's magnetic and attentive in person, then leaves Carrie waiting in the gaps, including the famous Paris disappearance where he simply stops showing up. He's the classic case of a man who can be fully there and then fully gone, with nothing in between to explain the switch.

characters.name: Don Draper
characters.why: He literally vanishes for days, leaves rooms mid-conversation, and treats disappearing as a coping strategy for anything uncomfortable. The women in his life are left to guess where he is and what he feels, because he'd rather leave than say.

characters.name: Jess Mariano
characters.why: He's tender and intense with Rory, then leaves town without telling her, and the first time she learns about it is after the fact. He's proof that a man can feel deeply and still handle it by running instead of talking.

characters.name: Chuck Bass
characters.why: He'll swear devotion and then disappear when things get real, leaving Blair to sort out what happened on her own. His silences are strategic, and he always assumes he can walk back in when it suits him.

interested.point: He replies within a normal window and keeps the thread alive
interested.detail: A man who's into you doesn't make you wait a day to hear back about dinner. If he asks you a question and then answers yours, you're looking at someone who's actually present.

interested.point: He makes plans with a day, a time, and a place
interested.detail: 'Thursday at 7 at that Thai place' beats 'we should hang soon' every single time. Real interest comes with logistics because he wants it to actually happen.

interested.point: He texts first without being prompted
interested.detail: If you're always the one starting the conversation, you're running a one-woman operation. An interested man sends the 'saw this and thought of you' without being asked.

interested.point: He follows through on small things
interested.detail: If he says he'll call after his meeting, he calls after his meeting. Reliability in tiny moments is how you know the big promises mean something.

interested.point: He tells you when he's busy and says when he'll be back
interested.detail: 'Slammed until Wednesday, can I call you Thursday?' is a man who values you enough to explain the gap. A Ghost never does that, because explaining would mean owning it.

interested.point: He stays consistent after the first thrill wears off
interested.detail: Anyone is attentive in week one. The signal is that week five looks like week one, with the same effort and the same curiosity.

not_interested.point: His replies are getting shorter and further apart
not_interested.detail: The slide from paragraphs to 'haha' to a thumbs-up isn't a busy season, it's a loss of interest. A man who wants to talk to you finds the thirty seconds.

not_interested.point: He views your story but ignores your message
not_interested.detail: He has time to watch your dinner but not to answer 'how was your day?' That's a choice, and it's rarely about the phone.

not_interested.point: He never confirms the plan
not_interested.detail: 'Let me check and get back to you' with no follow-up means he's keeping his options open or letting it die. Either way, he's not planning around you.

not_interested.point: He stops asking you questions
not_interested.detail: If the conversation is just you narrating and him reacting, he's no longer curious. Curiosity is the first thing to go when interest does.

not_interested.point: He answers the question but adds nothing
not_interested.detail: 'Good, you?' and 'Same' are polite, not engaged. People who like you offer extra, like a detail, a joke, or a follow-up.

not_interested.point: He only appears late at night or when it's convenient
not_interested.detail: A 'you up?' on a Saturday at 11pm after three days of silence is not interest, it's availability. He's reaching for you when it costs him nothing.

red_flags.point: The reply time keeps stretching
red_flags.detail: It goes from 20 minutes to 4 hours to a day, and he never mentions it or apologizes. That slow drift is how Ghosts test how little effort you'll accept.

red_flags.point: He's vague about his actual life
red_flags.detail: You don't know his schedule, his friends, or what he's doing this weekend, and he doesn't offer. A man who's building something with you lets you see some of his world.

red_flags.point: He has a history of 'it just fizzled' with every woman
red_flags.detail: Every ex is 'crazy' or 'it just ended,' and no one ever got an actual conversation. Count the times he tells that story, because you're the next chapter.

red_flags.point: He vanishes after a moment of closeness
red_flags.detail: You had a great date, an emotional talk, or a weekend together, and then three days of silence. The retreat after intimacy is the signature move.

red_flags.point: He apologizes with no explanation
red_flags.detail: 'Sorry, I've been so bad at texting' is a shrug, not accountability. If nothing changes after the apology, it's a script.

red_flags.point: He gets defensive when you name the pattern
red_flags.detail: 'Wow, I didn't realize you were keeping score' is deflection, not an answer. A man who cares says 'You're right, that wasn't fair to you.'

green_flags.point: He communicates before he disappears
green_flags.detail: 'I've got a rough week, I'll be quiet but I'm thinking of you' is the opposite of ghosting. Notice when he warns you instead of leaving you to guess.

green_flags.point: He can say 'I'm not feeling this' out loud
green_flags.detail: A man who can deliver a hard, kind no is rare and decent. That honesty means you'll never be left wondering.

green_flags.point: His words and actions line up over time
green_flags.detail: He says he'll call, he calls. He says he's busy, and then he's actually back on the day he said he'd be. Consistency is the cure for everything this man type does.

green_flags.point: He apologizes and then changes the behavior
green_flags.detail: One 'sorry I dropped the ball' followed by better effort is worth ten flowery apologies. Look for the change, not the speech.

green_flags.point: He's the same on a Tuesday as on a Saturday
green_flags.detail: His interest doesn't depend on mood, boredom, or whether anyone better is available. Steadiness is boring in the best way.

what_to_say.line: I've noticed the pace of your replies has changed. Are you still interested?
what_to_say.why: It's calm, factual, and gives him a clear chance to be honest. His answer, or his silence, tells you everything.

what_to_say.line: I'd rather hear a no than get no answer at all.
what_to_say.why: It names the standard without drama and makes the cost of silence visible. A decent man will respond; a Ghost will confirm himself.

what_to_say.line: I'm looking for someone who makes plans, so let me know if that's you.
what_to_say.why: It states what you want without begging for it. It hands him the decision and keeps your dignity intact.

what_to_say.line: Thanks for being honest. I'm going to step back.
what_to_say.why: It closes the loop on your own terms and doesn't wait for his permission. The exit is yours.

what_to_say.line: If you want to see me, I'm free Thursday. Otherwise, no worries.
what_to_say.why: It gives him one specific way to show interest and one easy way to opt out. You get information either way.

never_say.line: Did I do something wrong?
never_say.why: It puts you on trial for his silence and implies his behavior needs your explanation. The problem is his avoidance, not your texts.

never_say.line: I know you're busy, but I just wanted to check in again!
never_say.why: Over-explaining on his behalf teaches him that silence is free. You're doing his excuse-making for him.

never_say.line: Can you at least tell me why?
never_say.why: A man who ghosted you won't suddenly give a thoughtful answer, and asking hands him power over your closure. You'll wait for an explanation that doesn't come.

never_say.line: I'll wait for you to be ready.
never_say.why: It turns his avoidance into your patience project. You become a standby option with an open-ended deadline.

never_say.line: Fine, forget it. You're clearly a coward.
never_say.why: The anger is understandable, but it gives him a villain to point at and a reason not to look at himself. Your clean exit loses its power.

manipulation.name: The Soft Fade
manipulation.how_it_works: He reduces effort so gradually that no single moment feels worth confronting. By the time you notice, you're already questioning whether you're overreacting.
manipulation.defense: Track the trend, not the single text. If the last five days look worse than the first five, trust the line, not the explanation.

manipulation.name: The Busy Shield
manipulation.how_it_works: He uses 'work is crazy' to explain silence while staying active everywhere else. It sounds plausible, so you feel unreasonable pushing back.
manipulation.defense: Remember that busy people still send a sentence. Take him at his word and make your own plans without waiting.

manipulation.name: The Hot Return
manipulation.how_it_works: He reappears with warmth, a joke, and a 'miss you' that skips the explanation. The affection feels like an apology, so you let the gap go unaddressed.
manipulation.defense: Name the gap before you accept the warmth. 'Happy to hear from you, and I need to know what happened' keeps you in charge of the conversation.

manipulation.name: The Reverse Guilt
manipulation.how_it_works: When you ask about his silence, he turns it around: you're too intense, too fast, too much. You end up apologizing for a reasonable question.
manipulation.defense: Don't defend your expectations. 'That might be true, and I still need more consistency than you're giving' ends the debate.

manipulation.name: The Story Like
manipulation.how_it_works: He reacts to your posts but doesn't text, keeping you hopeful and in his orbit. It feels like contact, but it costs him nothing.
manipulation.defense: Treat a like as noise, not a signal. If you want, mute or limit him so his digital presence stops running your mood.

leverage.point: Your standard is the filter
leverage.detail: When you say 'I like plans and replies,' the Ghost either rises to it or exits on his own. Either result saves you months.

leverage.point: Stopping first takes the power back
leverage.detail: If you step away at the second dip, you skip the fade-and-wonder phase entirely. You end it on your schedule instead of his.

leverage.point: Silence works on him too
leverage.detail: A Ghost relies on your chasing to feel safe. When you stop initiating, he has to make an actual choice, and many of them reveal themselves in a week.

leverage.point: Specific asks reveal everything
leverage.detail: 'Dinner Saturday at 7?' is hard to dodge. His answer, a yes, a counter, or a wiggle, gives you data instead of mood.

leverage.point: Your full life is your strongest position
leverage.detail: When you're busy with friends, work, and plans, his absence stings less and your decisions get clearer. A full calendar makes it much harder for him to be your only story.

closest_cousin.text: The Love Bomber is the Ghost's loudest relative. Both end the same way, with silence where a person used to be, but the Love Bomber arrives with a flood of intensity, big declarations, and a speed that feels like destiny. The Ghost is usually quieter and more ordinary on the way in; his warmth is consistent rather than overwhelming, which makes his exit feel even more out of nowhere. The Love Bomber leaves after a dramatic peak, while the Ghost leaves after a perfectly nice Tuesday.
closest_cousin.tell: Look at the start: if the early weeks felt like a whirlwind of promises, he's a Love Bomber; if they felt pleasant and easy and then simply thinned out, he's a Ghost.

zombie.identity: He doesn't miss you. He misses having somewhere to go on a slow Tuesday, and you happen to be the grave he knows best.
summary: The Zombie is the man who vanished without a word and then, weeks or months later, rises with a message that sounds like nothing ever happened. 'Hey stranger.' 'Long time.' 'Was just thinking about you.' He treats the silence as weather, something that just rolled through, not a decision he made every single day he didn't text. He isn't always a bad guy. He's often charming, a little sheepish, and genuinely pleasant to talk to. What defines him is the gap between how casually he returns and how long he was gone.

Why does he do it? Mostly because reaching out is cheap and being accountable is expensive. Something in his life goes quiet: a breakup, a boring week, a birthday, a song, your name popping up in a story view. He gets a flicker of nostalgia or loneliness, and you're the easiest door to knock on because you were kind the last time. He rarely plans the return, which is why it feels so random. I can't tell you whether he truly misses you or just misses the feeling of being wanted. Honestly, he probably can't tell either. What I can tell you is that his interest follows his mood, not your effort, and that's the part you can act on.

Dating him feels like being haunted by a really nice memory. The reappearance gives you a rush: the relief, the vindication, the 'I knew he'd come back' glow. Then comes the whiplash of the old questions you thought you'd buried. Why did he leave? Is it different now? Do you ask? You start rehearsing the conversation in the shower. You feel petty for being hurt and foolish for being hopeful, and he benefits from both feelings because they keep you from demanding an explanation. The conversations are warm but strangely light, full of catching up and short on accounting.

It usually ends the way it began: with a slow fade into silence. A few good days, a flirty exchange, maybe one real date where he's lovely and attentive, then the replies stretch from minutes to hours to 'sorry, crazy week!' and then to nothing. Sometimes you get a second or third resurrection, each shorter and lazier than the last. It ends for good only when you stop answering the phone to the dead. The version that goes best for you is the one where you decide, calmly, that a man who returns without an explanation doesn't get to return at all.

text: His rhythm is feast, famine, feast. After a long silence he comes in warm and chatty, often late in the evening or on a weekend afternoon, when he's bored or sentimental. The openers are low-effort and high-charm: 'hey stranger,' 'random but I thought of you,' a meme, a song, a reaction to your story. He asks open, cozy questions like 'how've you been?' and 'what's new?' that invite you to do all the emotional lifting while he offers very little. Notice what's missing: any mention of the silence, any apology, any specific plan.

Over time the pattern tightens into a loop. The first few days are great: fast replies, a few flirty callbacks, a vague 'we should hang soon.' Then the plan stays vague, replies get shorter, and his messages migrate to reactions and emojis instead of sentences. When you push for specifics, he gets either breezy ('yes let's definitely do that!') or busy ('this week is nuts'). His tell is that his energy is high for texts and very low for logistics. A man who really wants to see you proposes a day and a time. A Zombie proposes a feeling.

threads.title: The Resurrection
threads.note: Four months of silence, zero acknowledgment, maximum charm.

bubbles.text: hey stranger 👀
Well, that's a name I haven't seen in a while.
I know, I know. Life's been insane. How are you??
I'm good. Busy, happy. What prompted the message?
Honestly just saw something that reminded me of you and smiled
We should catch up soon
Sure. Name a day and I'll check my calendar.
Haha okay let me see how this week shakes out and I'll let you know 🙌

threads.title: The Callout
threads.note: The moment you mention the gap, he turns it into your sensitivity.

bubbles.text: Before we catch up, I want to say it was strange when you stopped replying. I'd like to understand what happened.
Oh wow. Okay. I didn't realize it was a big deal
It wasn't huge, but it was noticeable. We were talking almost every day and then nothing for months.
I was dealing with a lot, I didn't mean anything by it. I thought we were just chilling
Chilling can include a text that says 'I'm swamped.'
I don't want to start things off on a heavy note, I really did miss talking to you
Can we just move forward? 🥺

threads.title: The Story View Revival
threads.note: He uses a low-stakes reaction to test whether the door is still open.

bubbles.text: 🔥🔥 that photo!!
Thanks! Didn't expect to hear from you.
You look amazing. Where was this?
A friend's wedding in Lisbon, a few weeks ago.
Lisbon!! I've always wanted to go. You'll have to tell me everything
Happy to. Coffee Saturday at 11?
Ahh Saturday might be tricky, I'll let you know
Anyway so jealous of that trip 😍

threads.title: The Clean Exit
threads.note: When she states what she needs, a Zombie either steps up or shuffles off.

bubbles.text: hey you. I've been thinking about you lately. Can we talk this week?
I'm open to talking. Last time we spoke, you went quiet for months. What's changed?
I know, that wasn't great. I was in a weird place
Thank you for saying that. If you want to see me, I need a real plan, not a maybe. Thursday at 7, dinner?
Thursday could work, I need to check my schedule though
I'll hold the spot until tomorrow at noon. After that I'll make other plans.
Wow okay, didn't realize it was a deadline 😅
Not a deadline, just clarity. Take care either way.

characters.name: Mr. Big
characters.why: He drifts in and out of Carrie's life for years, reappearing at the exact moment she's finally moved on. He's magnetic, vague about his reasons, and always assumes the door will still be open.

characters.name: Ross Geller
characters.why: Ross keeps circling back to Rachel with fresh nostalgia and a very elastic definition of what counts as a gap. His returns come from sincere feeling, but they run on his timeline and his version of events.

characters.name: Chuck Bass
characters.why: He disappears when things get real, then reappears with a grand gesture or a smirk, trusting charm to cover the absence. The comeback is always about his readiness, never about the damage he left behind.

characters.name: Edward Cullen
characters.why: He leaves without warning, goes silent for months, then returns with a dramatic explanation and an expectation of immediate forgiveness. The story is romantic, but she was the one left to pick up the pieces.

interested.point: He names the gap
interested.detail: He says something like 'I disappeared and that wasn't fair to you' before you have to raise it. A man who actually wants you back owns the silence first.

interested.point: He proposes a specific plan
interested.detail: 'Are you free Thursday at 7? I'll book that ramen place you mentioned.' Detail is the opposite of drifting.

interested.point: He reaches out when it's inconvenient
interested.detail: He texts on a Monday afternoon, not just at 11 p.m. on a Saturday. Interest that survives a busy schedule is real interest.

interested.point: He follows through on the small things
interested.detail: He said he'd call after his meeting and he does. Tiny proofs build back what the silence broke.

interested.point: He asks about the actual you
interested.detail: He remembers your sister's surgery or your job interview and asks how it went. Curiosity about your life beats a generic 'how've you been?'

interested.point: He stays consistent past the first week
interested.detail: The warmth doesn't evaporate once the novelty fades. Day twelve looks like day two.

not_interested.point: The only content is nostalgia
not_interested.detail: 'Remember that night in Brooklyn? Good times.' If he can only talk about the past and never the next date, he's visiting a memory, not you.

not_interested.point: He reacts but never initiates
not_interested.detail: Fire emojis on your stories, a heart on your photo, silence in your DMs. Low-effort contact is a way of staying present without being responsible.

not_interested.point: The plan is always 'soon'
not_interested.detail: 'We should totally hang soon!' with no day attached. Soon is the Zombie's favorite word because it costs him nothing.

not_interested.point: He texts late and never early
not_interested.detail: Nearly every message lands after 10 p.m. If you only exist when he's alone and bored, you're entertainment, not priority.

not_interested.point: He shrinks your question
not_interested.detail: When you ask about the silence he says 'I didn't think it was a big deal.' If he can't hold a mild question, he can't hold a relationship.

not_interested.point: His warmth falls off as you get specific
not_interested.detail: Flirty when it's vague, evasive when you ask for dinner Thursday. Enthusiasm that stops at logistics isn't enthusiasm.

red_flags.point: He pretends the silence didn't happen
red_flags.detail: He texts 'hey, what's up?' as if it's been a day, not four months. Erasing the gap means he's not planning to account for it, now or later.

red_flags.point: He makes your hurt the problem
red_flags.detail: 'Why are you making this so heavy?' or 'I didn't know you'd be upset.' When your reasonable reaction becomes the offense, the pattern is set to repeat.

red_flags.point: He returns in cycles
red_flags.detail: This is the third reappearance in a year, always after a quiet stretch in his love life. The timing says more than the words do.

red_flags.point: He wants the benefits without the commitment
red_flags.detail: He's happy to flirt and maybe hook up but gets slippery when you mention a date or a label. You're being used as a comfort, not chosen as a partner.

red_flags.point: His explanations keep changing
red_flags.detail: One text says work, another says family stuff, another says he was 'in a weird headspace.' Real reasons stay consistent, excuses shift.

red_flags.point: He disappears again after you give him a chance
red_flags.detail: You open up, plan the date, rearrange your week, and he goes silent the next day. The second death is always worse than the first.

green_flags.point: He apologizes without being asked
green_flags.detail: 'I went quiet and left you hanging. I'm sorry. Here's what I got wrong.' It's specific, short, and doesn't ask you to reassure him.

green_flags.point: He lets you set the pace
green_flags.detail: When you say you want to take things slow, he says 'okay, I'll earn it.' He doesn't pout or pressure.

green_flags.point: His actions match his words for weeks
green_flags.detail: He texts when he says he will, shows up on time, and the pattern holds long after the excitement fades.

green_flags.point: He can explain without excuses
green_flags.detail: 'I was avoiding a hard conversation and I handled it badly.' That's an adult accounting for himself, not a story to win you back.

green_flags.point: He wants to be known by your people
green_flags.detail: He's open to meeting your friends or sharing his plans with his own. Wanting to be witnessed is the opposite of a haunting.

what_to_say.line: It's good to hear from you. Before we catch up, I'd like to know what the silence was about.
what_to_say.why: It's warm, direct, and puts the burden of explanation on him. How he answers tells you nearly everything.

what_to_say.line: I'm open to seeing you. Can you do Thursday at 7?
what_to_say.why: A specific invitation separates real interest from nostalgia. Either he says yes or his vagueness reveals itself.

what_to_say.line: I'm not available for hot-and-cold. If you want to date me, I need consistency.
what_to_say.why: It states a standard, not a demand. A man who is serious will take that as information, not an attack.

what_to_say.line: I appreciate the apology. What would be different this time?
what_to_say.why: It invites him to move from sentiment to behavior. Anyone can say sorry; a plan is harder to fake.

what_to_say.line: I'm going to pass for now. I wish you well.
what_to_say.why: Short, kind, and final. It denies him the argument he's hoping for and leaves your dignity intact.

never_say.line: I've missed you so much, I didn't know if you'd ever text me again.
never_say.why: It tells him the door was open the whole time and the wait was painful. He learns that disappearing costs him nothing.

never_say.line: It's fine, don't worry about it.
never_say.why: It isn't fine, and saying so erases your own boundary. He'll take the free pass and use it again.

never_say.line: Why did you ghost me? What did I do wrong?
never_say.why: It turns his behavior into your fault and invites him to critique you. You're not on trial for being left.

never_say.line: Are we going to be something this time? I just need to know.
never_say.why: Asking for a label from a man who hasn't shown up consistently puts the weight on a promise he can't carry. Watch behavior first.

never_say.line: I'll wait until you're ready.
never_say.why: It makes you the open-ended waiting room. You're handing him the timeline and giving up yours.

manipulation.name: The Amnesia Opener
manipulation.how_it_works: He greets you as if no time has passed, trusting the warmth to bury the question. If you mention the gap, you're the one who 'brought down the vibe.'
manipulation.defense: Acknowledge the greeting, then name the gap in one calm sentence. Watch whether he engages or deflects.

manipulation.name: The Nostalgia Pull
manipulation.how_it_works: He floods you with shared memories, inside jokes, and 'remember when' moments that reconnect you emotionally before he's earned it. It feels like intimacy but it's an echo of the past, not a plan for the future.
manipulation.defense: Enjoy the memory, then ask a forward question: 'What would you want this to look like now?' If he stalls, the nostalgia was the whole offer.

manipulation.name: The Busy Shield
manipulation.how_it_works: He cites work, family, or a rough patch to explain the silence, giving a reason without any accountability. The excuse sounds sympathetic so you hesitate to push back.
manipulation.defense: Answer with empathy, then note the mechanics: 'Busy happens, and so does a two-line text.' Hold the standard without making it a fight.

manipulation.name: The Hot Restart
manipulation.how_it_works: He ramps up flirting, compliments, and big talk right away so the intensity outruns your doubts. You get swept into a mini honeymoon that makes the earlier abandonment feel irrelevant.
manipulation.defense: Match his pace to his actions, not his words. If he's moving fast in text but slow in plans, slow your own responses to match.

manipulation.name: The Guilt Flip
manipulation.how_it_works: When you hesitate or set a boundary, he says 'wow, I just wanted to say hi' or 'I guess I can't do anything right.' The goal is for you to apologize and drop the issue.
manipulation.defense: Stay level: 'I'm glad you reached out, and I still need consistency.' You can be kind and unmoved at once.

leverage.point: Your response time is a resource
leverage.detail: If you answer in four minutes every time, you teach him you're always on standby. Replying when it suits you restores the balance and shows him that access has a value.

leverage.point: Specificity filters him fast
leverage.detail: Offering one clear date and time makes a vague man either rise or retreat. You don't need to argue, because the invitation does the testing.

leverage.point: Your calm is more powerful than your anger
leverage.detail: A Zombie expects either drama or a warm welcome back. When you meet him with polite clarity, he has nothing to push against and has to show who he is.

leverage.point: A full life is the best boundary
leverage.detail: If your week is packed with friends, work, and plans you love, he doesn't get to reshape it on a whim. 'I'm free Thursday, not tonight' signals you're not waiting on his schedule.

leverage.point: You can say no to the second resurrection
leverage.detail: You are allowed to leave the message unanswered or the call unreturned. Declining to reopen the door is a complete answer, and it gives him zero chance to redefine it.

closest_cousin.text: The Boomerang is the Zombie's nearest relative because both men leave and come back, but they return for different reasons. The Boomerang comes back with a pitch: he misses you, he made a mistake, he wants to try again, so the conversation is at least about the relationship. The Zombie comes back with a pleasantry and no case at all, as if the absence needs no explanation and your being available is the point. The Boomerang tends to be dramatic and the Zombie tends to be breezy, and the breeziness is what makes him harder to confront.
closest_cousin.tell: The Boomerang returns with a speech about you; the Zombie returns with a casual hello that is really about his own boredom.

avoidant-poet.identity: He'll write you a midnight paragraph that makes your chest ache, then somehow be unable to confirm Thursday.
summary: The Avoidant Poet is the man who feels everything out loud and acts on almost none of it. He quotes the lyric, sends the voice memo from the train, and remembers the thing you said about your grandmother's kitchen three weeks ago. He's articulate about emotion in a way most men never bother to be, and that is exactly why he's so hard to read. You meet a person who seems to have a direct line to his heart, so you assume the line also connects to his calendar, his phone, and his Saturday. It doesn't. His feelings live in language, and language is the one place where nothing is asked of him.

Why does he do it? We can't see inside his head, and he may not fully know himself, but the pattern is consistent. Closeness in words is safe, because words can be edited, softened, and walked back. Closeness in action is binding: showing up on time, introducing you to friends, answering on a bad day. Many Poets seem to treat intensity as a substitute for intimacy, as if one devastating paragraph covers the cost of three ordinary weeks. He may truly mean every word when he writes it. The trouble is that meaning something at 1 a.m. and living it at 4 p.m. on a Wednesday are different skills, and he has only practiced the first.

Dating him feels like being adored by weather. When the sun is out, you feel seen in a way that makes everyone else seem blunt and boring. Then it clouds over: he goes quiet for four days, cancels with a beautifully worded apology, or says he's 'processing' something he never explains. You start rereading his old messages like scripture, hunting for proof that the deep thing is real. It probably is real, in its way. But you begin to notice you're in a relationship with his best sentences, not with the man who has to show up for them. And you become oddly skilled at translating his silence into something kinder than it is.

It usually ends not with a fight but with a slow fade into poetry. You finally ask for something concrete, like a plan, a label, or a consistent Tuesday, and he answers with a gorgeous, vague paragraph about how he's not ready, how you deserve more, how it's him. It sounds so tender that leaving feels cruel, so you stay a month longer than you should. When it does end, he'll probably miss you sincerely and text something heartbreaking in three weeks. That's the ending to plan for: he doesn't turn into a villain, he becomes a lovely, recurring ache. The kindest thing you can do for yourself is judge him by the verbs, not the adjectives.

text: His rhythm is feast or famine. You'll get nothing for two days, then a long, lyrical message at 11:40 p.m. that begins with 'I've been thinking about what you said…' His texts are rich in imagery and thin on logistics: you'll learn that he thinks you're 'a lit window in a city he can't afford,' but not what time he's free Friday. The tells are consistent. He answers feelings with feelings and questions about plans with fog ('let's see where the week goes'). He apologizes in advance for his own absence ('I'm bad at this, but I'm trying'), which quietly turns his unreliability into a trait you're expected to accept rather than a choice he's making. Long messages arrive after silence, never before it, as if the paragraph pays off the debt.

Over time the poetry stays but the frequency drops, and your messages start doing the heavy lifting. Early on he'll match your energy in bursts. Later you're the one proposing dates, checking in, and softening your questions so they don't feel like pressure. Watch the ratio of words to actions: if each month brings more beautiful texts and fewer actual evenings together, the story isn't deepening, it's just being retold. When he does sense you pulling back, expect a rush of tenderness, a song link, a 'you're so important to me,' and then the same pattern restarting by the weekend. The change that matters isn't in his language. It's whether a text ever ends with a time, a place, and him actually there.

threads.title: The 1 a.m. Confession
threads.note: Intensity at night, retreat by morning: his feelings are real but they don't survive daylight.

bubbles.text: I can't sleep. I keep replaying the way you laughed tonight, like the whole room tilted toward it. I don't say this stuff easily, but you feel like a place I've been looking for.
Okay that is the loveliest thing anyone's texted me in a long time. I felt it too. 🥹
Good. I wanted you to know. It's strange how clear everything feels at this hour.
Want to get dinner Thursday? I'd love to keep this going in person.
Morning! Thursday still sounds good to me. Does 7:30 work?
Hey. Sorry, my head's a lot today. Last night was real, I just need to sit with it.
Sit with it and tell me about Thursday? I'm not asking for a verdict, just dinner.
Let me see how the week unfolds. I don't want to promise something I can't feel into yet.

threads.title: The Plan That Dissolves
threads.note: He agrees in spirit and avoids the specifics, so you end up with a mood instead of a plan.

bubbles.text: Are we still on for Saturday? I'm about to book the table.
I love that you're planning something. Honestly it's one of my favorite things about you.
Thank you! So Saturday at 8?
I want to be there in the way you deserve. Can I confirm closer to it?
Closer to it meaning when? The restaurant needs a headcount.
Friday afternoon, I think. I just don't want to force a Saturday-shaped version of me.
I'll wait until Friday at noon. After that I'm making other plans.
That's fair. You're allowed to protect your time. I'm sorry I make this feel so heavy.

threads.title: The Define-the-Relationship Talk
threads.note: He honors the feeling and dodges the commitment, and his tenderness makes the dodge hard to challenge.

bubbles.text: I want to ask something and I'd like a straight answer. Where do you see this going?
I feel more with you than I've felt in years. I just struggle with how words like 'exclusive' flatten something this alive.
I hear that. I'm not asking for a poem, though. Are you seeing other people?
No. God, no. There's no one else. I just don't want to build a cage around something that's still becoming itself.
A label isn't a cage. For me it's just knowing I'm not guessing every week.
I understand that. I think I need more time to feel safe enough to say it.
How much more time? A week? A season? I need an actual sense of it.
I wish I could give you a date. That's the part I hate about myself.

threads.title: The Return After Five Days
threads.note: He reappears with beauty instead of accountability, and the real test is whether you accept the poem in place of the apology.

bubbles.text: I walked past the bookstore where we first talked about Rilke and thought of you. Still thinking of you, actually.
That's sweet. It's also been five days without a word from you.
I know. I went somewhere quiet inside myself and I didn't know how to come back with anything worth saying.
You didn't need to say anything profound. A 'hey, I'm having a rough week' would've been enough.
That's fair. I tend to disappear when I care most. It's a flaw, I know.
It's a pattern, and it affects me. Are you actually going to change it, or just describe it well?
That's a hard question, and I don't want to answer it badly.
Then answer it slowly, but answer it. I'm not available for more silent weeks.

characters.name: Don Draper
characters.why: He can write a pitch that makes a room weep about longing and love, yet he can't be honest with the women he's actually with. His eloquence is a way of staying unreachable, and each woman gets the poetry while the real man stays offstage.

characters.name: Mr. Big
characters.why: He gives Carrie dazzling, cinematic moments and then goes silent the instant things need to become ordinary and committed. His feelings are real, but they get expressed in gestures and grand returns rather than steady, accountable presence.

characters.name: Edward Cullen
characters.why: His devotion arrives in sweeping, tortured declarations, yet he repeatedly leaves, withdraws, and decides alone what the relationship can bear. He turns his own fear into a tragic romance and expects her to find that more moving than inconsistent.

characters.name: Jess Mariano
characters.why: He's the brooding, book-quoting boy whose emotional depth is obvious to everyone except the version of him that has to communicate it. When Rory needs him to say the plain, brave thing, he disappears instead, and the literate ache is mostly what remains.

interested.point: He lets you see the unpolished poem
interested.detail: An interested Poet shows you the draft, not just the finished stanza: he admits he's nervous, or that he rewrote a text four times. The tell is vulnerability that costs him something rather than flatters him.

interested.point: His words come with times attached
interested.detail: He doesn't just say 'I want to see you.' He says 'Thursday, 7:30, I'll book it.' When his feelings get a calendar slot, you're seeing the rare version where the inner life crosses into the outer one.

interested.point: He reaches out before the silence gets long
interested.detail: A short 'Rough day, but thinking of you, talk tomorrow' beats a brilliant paragraph after four days of nothing. Interest shows up in the repair, not the rhetoric.

interested.point: He introduces you to the real parts of his life
interested.detail: You meet his friend, see his apartment, or get invited to his brother's thing, and it's not hidden behind a mood. A man who lets you into the ordinary is moving beyond the romantic idea of you.

interested.point: He can name his pattern and act against it
interested.detail: He says, 'I tend to go quiet when I'm overwhelmed, so I'm going to tell you when it happens,' and then he does. Insight that changes behavior is the whole difference between a poet and an alibi.

interested.point: He follows through on small, boring things
interested.detail: He remembers to send the address, pick the restaurant, or return the book on the day he said he would. The small, unglamorous promises are the real love letters with this type.

not_interested.point: The beauty goes up while the contact goes down
not_interested.detail: His messages get more lyrical as his availability shrinks, so you receive an exquisite paragraph in place of a Friday night. When the prose is doing the work the presence should be doing, he's managing you.

not_interested.point: He answers plans with weather reports
not_interested.detail: 'Let's see how the week feels' is a mood, not a commitment. A man who's interested picks a day, and a man who's hovering stays in the forecast.

not_interested.point: He apologizes for who he is instead of changing what he does
